We had security problems, so it was impossible to have daily conversations with every municipality and every town, and it was quite normal to set up regions which would draw together a certain area, and it was much easier to communicate with their representatives then from the party. In this respect, the Posavina region was established, the Central Bosnia region and Herzegovina also set up its own. But they were homogenous and compact from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You dealt with one or both, as you've spoken of the principle, but the Bosnia and Posavina was created first and then Herceg-Bosna was second?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I think that on the 11th of November, the Posavina region was set up, the Travnik region on the 14th of November, and Herceg-Bosna on the 18th. But I was not invited to any of these gatherings, nor did I attend them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, what was the first you learned of the creation of these two communities?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, I think they sent a fax message to the party, so it was no surprise that the Posavina and Travnik community were established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just returning briefly to your instruction to Kordic to attend your office for fear of being arrested. Did you get a response from Dario Kordic --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I think he didn't come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did he write to you, do you know? It's Exhibit 21,1.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I don't know. If you show me the text, I might recall it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 21,1, and also 25,1, please. First of all, 21,1. And if there's a B/C/S version of it, can that be made available to the witness. Is there a B/C/S version attached to that? He may need to look at the B/C/S version, I think.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any comment to make about it? Any expression of whether your views and his coincided?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No, I think that at that time, while I was in charge of the government policy and the central policy in Sarajevo, people in the field were slowly setting up a para-organisation because they did not like the vertical structure of things, and each of them thought that from their local perspective they could create policy. This failure to respect the documents adopted and the party leadership was soon to be expressed when there was an open confrontation between two currents in the HDZ and when many personal ambitions surfaced, so that even attempts to hold meetings together with President Tudjman were able to reconcile these two currents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll be coming to that very shortly, but to try to keep things chronological so far as possible, could you just look, please, now, at 25,1, already produced. If you follow the B/C/S, this is from Dario Kordic, or signed by him on behalf of the regional community of Herzegovina in Travnik, a reply to the proposal for a separate meeting of the Croatian regional community of Travnik. And if you would just like to remind yourself of the B/C/S original.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any comment on this document?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It speaks of a lack of coordination between the main offices in Zagreb, Sarajevo, Herzegovina, and Travnik and speaks of possible negative repercussions resulting from the different approach of certain people, and so on. Was there an identity of views between the local community and you, or not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Even if it existed formerly, many people on the ground acted differently from what was in the political programme of the HDZ and from the policy of the presidency of the HDZ. And as regards the poor level of subordination, you should know that this was the most tragic period of the war in Croatia, and it was a time when the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina was already beginning, when the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, was burning and destroying Croatian villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did either of these local communities have the structural or the constitutional right to be dictating what the presidency should be doing?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No, they did not. They mostly dealt with local problems, and their task was to prepare the defence of the Croatian people from aggression. Let me remind you, the former Yugoslavia had two kinds of army and weapons. One kind was the official army, which was already instrumentalised by Milosevic and the Serbian fascists, and the other system was the system of All People's Defence, something that William Tell advocated his time, and it was supposed to defend local citizens in the area where they lived. However, with the exception of Slovenia, no republic was ever given those weapons. The communist authorities, before the democratic elections, gave the weapons of the All People's Defence to the Yugoslav People's Army. After that, the Yugoslav army openly armed Serb citizens in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well, and the role of the regional HDZ communities was to prepare people and mobilise people for defence as far as was possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next document, please, is one that's already been -- no, is one that has a regular exhibit number, Z30, has yet to be produced. May he have that in the original, and perhaps the original had better be placed on the ELMO, because I'm going to ask the witness to read a couple of passages from it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we turn to the passages, just confirm, please, that this is an excerpt from the minutes of the 28th of November of 1991 of the presidency.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you turn -- in the English version it's the second sheet; in the B/C/S, it is the second sheet and the third sheet. On the second sheet, the penultimate paragraph, the second subparagraph of paragraph (a) begins "HDZ BiH." Could you please read that out for us?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: [Translation of Serbo-Croatian document as read] "Conclusion from the minutes of the 14th of November 1991 that serious problems and differences of opinion have arisen in the leadership of the BH HDZ with regard to political activity and the realisation of the programmatic principles is rendered more precise, as follows. The BH HDZ is a united party operating on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina within the scope of the AVNOJ borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but represents a constituent part of the Croatian Democratic Union based in Zagreb, as expressly established in the statutory provisions and the programmatic principles."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you then turn to subparagraph (c), over the page. Read that -- at least, just read the first three lines and one word.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: [Translation of Serbo-Croatian document as read] "The presidency of the BH HDZ unanimously adopts the decision on the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna of 18th November, 1991, which represents the freely expressed will of the Croatian people and which consists of the following municipalities."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They are then listed, and the last line and half of subparagraph C reads ...

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: [Translation of Serbo-Croatian document as read] "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna represents a political, cultural, economic, and territorial entity."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you go down, please, to subparagraph (e), and in particular the second subparagraph of that paragraph, beginning "Formirane."

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. [Translation of Serbo-Croatian document as read] "The established Croatian communities are independent political, cultural, economic, and territorial entities which have their own organs to represent them and act on their behalf."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document, I think, that you signed. Did it carry your full consent and will with it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: There was a big struggle, and a compromise was reached. They conceded that we are fighting for Bosnia and Herzegovina within the AVNOJ borders, which means for the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I agreed to recognise Herceg-Bosna, but what does the expression "political organisation" mean? In the former Yugoslavia, a women's association, a trade union, a youth organisation was such an organisation. Furthermore, it says that they are to represent a region, which is completely true, because the presidency of the HDZ and the people in the government and in the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina were representing the republic, and at that time, no one suggested -- and it would probably not have been adopted if they had -- that they represent administrative institutions, because we had, within the state, legal institutions such as municipalities, and the local governments, and various government committees, because if they had demanded something like this, it would have meant the creation of para-state institutions, which, at that time, no one would have accepted officially. So we had to mitigate the public response to this, because the Serbs and their propaganda, when they were setting up their own so-called autonomous regions, said that the creation of Herceg-Bosna was a parallel system, which was a new incentive to those who wanted to destroy Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state. By emphasising that we were still fighting for a united Bosnia-Herzegovina and that this was a regional community with economic and cultural responsibilities, I succeeded in mitigating the public response to the creation of this community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The next document is 2746. Nothing to say about it, just note that it is the minutes of the presidency meeting of the 17th of December.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's an old document, dating to 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this document we don't have in translation. Can you just tell us what it is? It appears to be dated, I think, the 22nd of December.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Ever since the HDZ was founded in Mostar, the situation has been complicated, and there were very many personal conflicts. This is one of the reports submitted by Damjan Vlasic, and it relates to the situation in Mostar, all sorts of problems and strife, and that it is impossible --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll stop you there, unless it has any bearing on the issues with which you know we are more closely concerned, and unless there is anything that you want to add that takes it away from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. It's quite irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Summary paragraph 19, paragraph 19, on the 23rd of December, was there a meeting of the Community of Herceg-Bosna's presidency, including Boban and Dario Kordic, at Tomislavgrad in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I don't know, because I was not present at that meeting. However, several days later, I heard such a meeting had taken place. I'd never been invited to that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you hear happened at it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No, it was -- the meeting was always mentioned, but I never learned anything about the contents of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then the next meeting that I want you to deal with in detail is the 27th of December of 1991. Where was that meeting, and who was present, and so on?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: The meeting was held in Zagreb on the official premises of the President of the Republic of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman. In addition to President Tudjman, there were also Stipe Mesic, Josip Manolic, Dalibor Brozovic, Dr. Milan Ramljak, Gojko Susak, Ante Beljo, and several other officials of the party, and the Croatian government were present on the Croatian side. On our side, there were all officials discharging individual offices in the government and presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and presidents of very many regional boards, even though I need to say that we arrived there separately and that we also left Zagreb separately, because it was on the eve of peace in Croatia; that is, on the 2nd of January, '92, peace was to be signed in Sarajevo between Croatian Serbs, UNPROFOR, and representatives of the Republic of Croatia and the Croatian army. So on the 27th, we all met in Zagreb, but it was already clear by that time that there were two factions in the HDZ and that the faction rallied around Herceg-Bosna had shown they did not comply with the adopted and agreed political programme. Among other things, they in particular wanted to disparage, to belittle my person, my political activity, my political commitment, even though President Tudjman at that very meeting said that I had done a great deal for the results achieved until that particular time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'd like you, please, to look at three documents which we must explain to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First there's the largest, the fattest document, which is 2717. I think you may find it third, but just -- will you hand that to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is this?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: These are the minutes of that meeting held on the 27th of December, 1991, in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I come to look at those and to deal with them in whatever method may be acceptable to the Tribunal, can I explain that you should have two other documents -- it may not be necessary to trouble the witness with these, but they'll assist the Tribunal with what I think has gone to the Defence -- I certainly hope it has -- 2717,1, if the Tribunal and my friends opposite have that, is an extract from the minutes which was served, and 2717,1A is a partial translation of some of the elements of that document, I think. So that explains, I hope, the documents, and if there's anything that's wanted in more detail, I'll explain it. I don't think Mr. Kljujic need be particularly troubled with that, but that's what there is there, in case it assists.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I think that Document 2717,1 is part of the Document 2717.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, given the lack of a complete translation of the minutes, and given the proper restraints on the interpreters in the booths, all that I can do is find the passages in the full minute, ask the witness to read them, and they will therefore translate them to us over the headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you want to go beyond what's in 2717,1A?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think there are one or two more passages beyond that, yes. In any event, it may be helpful to find our way around the larger document in case it becomes of significance later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at the larger document, let's focus on 2717, Mr. Kljujic, we see that the first four pages are page-numbered. Have it in front of you, and we'll put the appropriate pages on. We see the first page is not numbered, then the second, third, and fourth pages are numbered. Thereafter, the numbering is either different or has gone. Can you just explain that? If you can't explain it, don't guess.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I can, but it must be a technical error or something, because I did not make this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, now if we go, please, through the document very swiftly, but we'll just physically count pages because they aren't numbered and it's the only way to be sure we reach the right pages, but we see that on the second sheet which is numbered page 2, your name at the beginning -- I beg your pardon -- at the foot of the page, and then there's a long or fairly long extract attributed to you. Did you speak at an early stage of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I did, several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we then go to a page in the top left-hand corner differently numbered 7/3/JG --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where are we finding this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's on the top left-hand corner. You can see some numbers, "7/3/JG".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, who was speaking at this time? If you need to check by going back a few pages, about three or four pages, do so and you'll see who was speaking.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Returning to part of what he said on page 7/3/JG, would you pick it up at the middle of the page, the beginning of the paragraph "Znaci"? Read it to us, and the interpreters will interpret it for us.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: [Translation of Serbo-Croatian document as read] "And so on the survival of the sovereignty of Bosnia under present-day conditions is, from the Croatian point of view, such that we may not promote it. We may not even postulate it openly. We may not postulate it openly, but why not accept this offer of demarcation, since that is in the interests of the Croat people, of the Croat people here in this republic and the Croat people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, for I see no reason which would be a serious-enough reason which would go against it, all the more so during the talks which I personally conducted both with Izetbegovic and with Milosevic and, moreover, one of our people in Bosnia has drawn up this proposal on such a demarcation where the Croat areas and those which you encompassed in this community of Herceg-Bosna and in the community of Croatian Sava river valley where, in case of demarcation, in addition to these two communities, Croatia would get, presumably for due political reasons, both the Cazin and Bihac area, and that will be almost full satisfaction, optimal satisfaction, of Croat --" I guess it is "interests", but there is a word missing -- "national interests, not only at present but also in the future, and that then from the remaining part --" and that's the end of the quotation. It's interrupted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then the next page?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: [Translation of Serbo-Croatian document as read] "Then from the remaining part where mostly Muslims will stay and a part of Catholic Croats, so in other words that around Sarajevo, one can create a little state, a statelet (phoen) which would remind of that historical countrylet (phoen) of Bosnia which would then be a buffer zone between this demarcation line between Serbia and Croatia and which would, under those conditions, necessarily rely on Croatia for the major part. "International factors could be satisfied with that, as they must be counting on it quite seriously. As you have just mentioned, they are now counting also on this Serb gendarme, vis-à-vis that Muslim element, that Islamic element in the territory of Yugoslavia, whose aspiration is to found an Islamic state in Europe with the support of Teheran and Tripoli."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was still Tudjman speaking, was it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you turn over one sheet, please, to 8/2 and pick up what Boban says at the foot of the page?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: [Translation of Serbo-Croatian document as read] "Founding municipalities HA --" I don't know what "HA" means -- "and community Herceg-Bosna now have, according to a census, 55 per cent of Croats altogether. There are 27 per cent of Muslims, 9 per cent Serbs, and the rest are others. "However, since the municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina are along more or less the same lines as in Croatia where established, so in a way which would combine the Serb and the Muslim population in the Croatian territory, or vice versa, by cleansing the border areas which are, in fact, at the border areas of Herceg-Bosna, this creates about 65 per cent of the Croat population in Herceg-Bosna. "Excuse me, as I know the latest data in Serbia are 63 per cent."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The word "cleansing" was used there. Was that a regular term used in political discussion at that time or not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was its meaning when used in meetings of this type?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Under the Communist regime, the municipalities with the Croat majority were often administratively abolished or subdivided so that one half would come under another municipality and the other half under a third municipality. In those expanded municipalities, the Croats would then come to be a minority. There are a series of such examples in Dobratici, between Jajce and Travnik, and Kotor Varos, the municipalities of Ravne, then the municipality of Ivanjska near Banja Luka, and so on and so forth. In 1967, those municipalities which were Croat were split up and placed, by and large, under Serb domination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we go to page 16/4, it's just about a little over halfway through, this is at the foot of the page of 16/4. This is what Dario Kordic was saying, and if you can -- or a summary of what he was saying. Can you read that out, please?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: [Translation of Serbo-Croatian document as read] "Mr. President, distinguished participants, Dario Kordic, president of the municipality board of the HDZ of Busovaca, the chairman of the Travnik Regional Community, of the Croat Democratic Community and vice-president of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna. I shall speak. "It is my duty and my privilege on behalf of the one which some call a disputable part about Dobratici and Jajce to Kraljeva, Sutjeska and Vares. "For six months we deliberated your idea of the 13th and the 20th June in blood, and we've just --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just stop for two seconds. The Court can follow this on page 6 of the English extract, if it prefers to do it that way, rather than following it on the screen. I'm sorry to have interrupted you, Mr. Kljuic. Please pick it up again. "The 20th of June in blood," you were on.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: [Translation of Serbo-Croatian document as read] "I should say that the Croat spirit here in these lands of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna and the Sava Valley, during those 40 days and notably in Bosnia, this is the proclamation of the Croat Community at Grude has strengthened more than for a year following the elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina. "The Croat people in this regional/ subregional community lives with the idea of the final incorporation joining with the Croatian state and is prepared to do it with all the means and Croat spirit which boils in young men. "I'm saying this because I come from the field. We visited every village in the territory of this subregional community of Herceg-Bosna. "I should say I'm sorry that many leaders from the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina were not with their people in these areas during Christmas holidays and seen numerous Croat standards on Croat homes in these municipalities of the Bosnian part. There were 60 to 70 flags in the municipalities. This was not noted down. "Although this is a sad Christmas because of the destruction of Croatia, this was the most Croat Christmas since the war in this part of Bosnia, and this is a fact that nobody may deny. "I should say that any option which would not mean clear demarcation of the Croat soil in the territory of Herceg-Bosna and the protection against the destruction of the Croat body, except through a clear state mechanism of the State of Croatia which would serve as a guarantor to the Herceg-Bosna Croats, would be treason, whether it happens in three months or a year, yet we must believe in it. "When some gentleman said that it is not true, that it is not a reality, what our fate would be, what was said about Travnik, I do not think that in other municipalities we would have even a relative majority unless we applied this concept. "I need to point out one thing in particular, and that is that the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina has been throughout only a side-show of the SDA policy. It was a surrogate of the Croatian policy. When the Croat being was reborn in the latter half of 1990, at the time of the elections in November, until November of 1991 when the resurrecting Croat being became a dying being and the Croat policy had no identity, it was the policy of subjects, it was passive, it was cowardly, as shown in the beginning of the dirty war in the State of Croatia and its transfer to the lands of Herceg-Bosna. The SDA leadership in these lands revealed all their honest intentions regarding a civil republic which they coloured with an unheard of Islamic fundamentalism of SDA leaders, spiced with the Congress of the Party of Democratic Action, and ovations to ambassadors of Turkey and Libya, Cengic's statement three days ago that their home is in Turkey, and the premature disclosure of the dream of the Jamahirija. "We, from mixed regions, are well familiar with the sincere intentions of the leaders of the Party for Democratic Action. "I am not an advocate of false peace because it necessitates a useless waste of energy. I believe what Mr. President said. This leadership, this peak of the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina and their government, are incapable of concluding this agreement with Muslims and Serbs because their point of departure is that we are not more than 17,4 per cent, and they do not take as the point of departure as to who we are, what our real strength is, which is our state, and how big is our power. "I believe that this leadership cannot put to life this new platform and that in this Croat Democratic Union, that is, the implementation of this policy cannot be provided by all these same people. "I should like to say that what we used to say at these meetings with our people had been, by the Muslims, ready to move in front of us, we would have fought with them. But at this particular point in time, we have no moral obligation to them because they do not deserve that, and we do not think that either Izetbegovic or his clique will be able to pursue even this Muslim policy in this territory of theirs which will remain, because they are driving the Muslim people to ruin. The Muslim people will depose them themselves because they did not provide them with the defensive mechanism, and their people will, at long last, understand that."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll finish this witness's evidence in chief, I take it, today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, yes. This is probably the longest passage, and there's only one sheet of the summary to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Half past 2.00. I'm sorry. Mr. Kljuic, could you be back, please, at half past 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25 1

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've just heard what Dario Kordic said at the meeting. By this time, what sort of a figure was he, to your knowledge? How important? How did his views fit with yours, or with others, and so on?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: He was not an important figure in the party until the time when Herceg-Bosna was established. I have to say that what I stood for and what I implemented as president was not just my personal position, but I also received full support in the elections, and then through the party, the platform adopted on the 23 and 24 March in Mostar, which was a unified and undivided Bosnia with equal representation of all, integral Bosnia and Herzegovina, which would be also equal to other republics in the Former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any personal relationship with Kordic, good or bad? Or not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Not particularly good or bad. Privately we did not have much communication, only through official channels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The views he expressed at this meeting, that we've just read out, do you want to comment on those at all?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I think that this was a position that was held by a faction which was led by Boban. In other words, I don't think that he said anything different from what Boban and some others had also stated, except perhaps in some details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll turn to things that were said by Tudjman, but there's one earlier passage that I ought to have asked you to deal with. I cut short a little too early the passage I was asking you to deal with. It's at page 8/1. In the middle of the page, "Sa toga," we've taken it to the end of the previous paragraph. Could you just read, picking up at "Sa toga," and go over to the following page?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: [Translation of Serbo-Croatian document as read] "From that point of view, even some kind of cantonisation with the rest of Bosnia and Herzegovina, for us it does not represent a solution which is the solution, which means the separation. So that is where the problem lies. So I believe that you have missed -- that you have been implementing a policy and politics which is, on the one side, to retain sovereignty, and the surrounding areas which may have been more interested for joining and which in the end the people are using to support the Croatian cause. So it seems to me that as we use this historical moment to create an independent and internationally recognised Croatia, I believe it is the time now also to use this moment to gather our Croatian national --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who is speaking here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I may have stopped you too quickly. Could you finish that sentence?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: [Translation of Serbo-Croatian document as read] "... which are in the borders which are as wide as possible." Now, I don't know whether this would involve 28 or 30 municipalities. I think that that is of lesser importance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Staying with President Tudjman, but moving to a later part of the minute, can we go to page -- it's about three-quarters of the way through, 21/2/VM. We see a paragraph headed with the word "President," I think, and then the first paragraph I needn't trouble you with, the first major paragraph, but if you could start with "Da Bosna," please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. [Translation of Serbo-Croatian document as read] "All the history has shown that Bosnia and Herzegovina is not a solution for the Croatian people. First of all, it was created by colonial conquest of an Asian power, gentlemen, let's not forget that, starting in the period between the 15th and 18th centuries, at the expense of Croatian people and the expense of Croatian territory. "All these colonial creations have collapsed both in Asia and Africa. Bosnia-Herzegovina did not exist between the two wars. Communists invented it after World War II, brought it back on stage. They even proclaimed the Muslims as a nation in order to ostensibly solve the dispute between the Croatian and Serbian peoples. Did they succeed in it? No, on the contrary. So one should not count with Bosnia and Herzegovina as something which was God-given, and something that is to remain, and not at all neglect how harmful it can be. "Croatia has been brought in an impossible situation, territorially speaking, because of the creation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We cannot create an independent Croatia both administratively, let alone defensively speaking. So what are the perspectives? What is the future of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina? I quoted -- I said that we have fallen from 24 to 17 per cent of the population. Mr. Vlasic, from Travnik, has said that in Travnik the population is down to 37 from 56. Be sure, if Bosnia-Herzegovina became independent, within ten years that will assume horrible proportions, because the Muslims are counting on demographic expansion, and because of their birth rate, they are counting on 500.000 Muslims from Turkey, and so on. So the survival of Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent and sovereign state, even if possible, would be at the expense of the Croatian people, and it would enable normal territorial creation of a Croatian state, and it also creates preconditions for disappearance of the Croatian peoples such as they exist in Bosnia and Herzegovina today. Furthermore, there is no one unified Bosnia and Herzegovina today."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That observation by Tudjman about the impossibility of Croatia existing in its then form and shape, is that something that he said just once or did he say it on other occasions?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: He said here, for the first time, explicitly this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] on other occasions?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Not in this form.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We move on two pages, I believe, to 22/1 LJ; still Tudjman speaking. The second-to-last paragraph on the page, the paragraph beginning with the word "Iz", could you just read that paragraph for us, please?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: [Translation of Serbo-Croatian document as read] "For tactical reasons, we support a sovereign Bosnia as long as it exists, but there is no more sovereign Bosnia. Serbs separated themselves out. You have no more power. The Bosnian government has no authority over the Serbian areas and the Serbian parts. Not only the Serbian parts of Bosnia but all of Bosnia-Herzegovina is involved in the war against Croatia, its territory, and the Serbian population against Croatia, that is a fact. So what do we talk --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all I require. Thank you very much. We turn now to some of the things that you were saying. It had been seen earlier, but can we turn to page 24/1 LJ. I think this is you speaking. I better check that it is. If you come back a couple of pages, I think you'll see that this is you speaking. Can you pick it up from the third paragraph, "Dalje"?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: [Translation of Serbo-Croatian document as read] "Further, we consider that we had to conduct discussions, but in all these discussions, gentlemen, everybody is asking the question, 'Who is the first? Who is going to propose the partition of Bosnia?' 'Let's see. You want cantonisation. Very well.' Because when we brought the Serbs to this to say, 'All right, you have initiated this, you don't want an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, so please draft a paper,' and they brought a paper with the Belgrade initiative because they have the media, and now the question is, 'Who is going to bite first?' "We were here the last time when you were here and you told us there were three options. The first one is to fight for a sovereign Bosnia as long as we can. Second, if the Serbs take control over their parts by force because it's under international control, let's have this rump Bosnia and Herzegovina in a confederation with Croatia. Then there will be a buffer zone. We will get the Muslims. "Then somebody said, and that was not very tactful, 'We will give the Muslims some kind of autonomy,' so let there be this type of Bosnia-Herzegovina, please."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then President Tudjman asked you something or said something, namely --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. It states here: [Translation of Serbo-Croatian document as read] "Stjepan, let's be specific now. Let's not waste --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you added?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: (In English) Just one minute, please. (Interpretation) "Let's not waste time, please," and I replied, "The third option -- let me just finish, Mr. President, the third option. The third is the Muslims do not want to go with us. The Serbs want their own. Let's engage in propaganda and that it is a question of Europe versus Balkans, Belgrade, Zagreb, and then we have a chance to get the Travnik Muslims, the Bugojno Muslims, the Jajce, and then Croatia could get a block, and this is what it should be prepared."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you therefore set out the three options. I see one or two other contributions. Can you turn over to 25/2 JG, please, towards the end. At the foot of this page, you can see "Miro Lasic". Can you just read what his contribution was, or part of it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: [Translation of Serbo-Croatian document as read] "If we manage to create a Bosnian dinar, believe me, the Serbs will drown in their own faeces of dinar. That is, if we manage to do this, and I'm not sure that we will be. "The President replies, 'You will not succeed. It is clear that you will not succeed. You will not. I suggest that we agree on a commission which will conduct these talks and which, in that sense, will be, if you will, the leadership of the Croatian Democratic Community in Bosnia. Do you have any suggestion, Kljuic, Boban, Stanic?'" He is from Bosnia. "'Indeed, these three have to be there. Let's go on.' Then somebody interjected, 'We have to include Bihac. Bihac is very important.' And another interjection, 'As I said, as a region it remains under our control.' "Stipe Mesic then says he is suggesting that it be where things are critical, and then an interjection, 'To be a negotiator where the situation is critical.'" The President says, "Who do you suggest," and then the interjection which is unintelligible. "Is he here? Stjepan, this is not a personal question but an issue of political positions." "Could you put Rajic?" "Why not put the professor from Travnik?" The president, "Well, I did not say it could not be. Go ahead." Kordic, and he joins in the discussion later, "I have the right to be here, because there are 12 municipalities behind me. I am the presiding officer of that regional community." Then the president, "Very well. Kljuic, Boban, Vlado Santic, we said that Iko Stanic, Udovicic, Vlasic, and who else?" And then an interjection, "Dario Kordic from Busovaca. That's seven, Kljuic, Boban, Vlado Santic, Iko Stanic, Udovicic, Vlasic, Kordic." "Very well, that is accepted." The last two names, I just want to say, are misspelled. "Let's vote. Who is for Kljuic?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's enough of that quotation. That grouping that was created at the end included Kordic, at his own suggestion?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No. In the end, a group was created, Kljuic, Boban, Stanic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there another body created at the end of this meeting, an inner-leadership body?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No, it was only said that in the future, since some of those from Herzegovina who were present and questioned my leadership in the party, they asked that a commission be represented on all these events, which would also include Boban and Stanic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can take you back to the reference, if necessary, but do you remember the contribution of Perica Juric and a reference to refugees?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall, but I believe it's in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of this meeting, what, if anything, was said, to your recollection, about what would happen to the Muslims and what the consequences for them would be? I'll take you to a reference, if you want to find one, that touches the topic, but first of all your memory.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Both factions in this meeting had their own views on the Muslims. My faction considered the Muslims an important partner in the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and considering the historical friendship, they were our only political friends. Boban's side viewed the Muslims with indignation, and later it would be shown that they frequently had contacts with the Serbs, regardless of the fact that during this very period, the Serbian fascism was at its cruellest against the Croatian people, not just in Vukovar but in Dubrovnik and in other parts of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We've heard something about President Tudjman's attitude towards Croatia's shape and the possibility of its survival in that shape. What, in general, if you can summarise it, was his attitude towards Croatia's borders and shape as expressed at this meeting or at other meetings?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: He said that for the first time openly, that Croatia's shape was not right and that it cannot stay that way, and that the HDZ policy, that is, the Zagreb policy, would be evidenced in Dayton when some of the best Croatian territory in Posavina was sacrificed for three municipalities that were very backward, that is, Dravar, Glamoc and Bosanski Grahovo. But let me go back to the main issue, which is that at this meeting and in the party itself, people split along the lines of those who did not believe that much in the significance of the Helsinki conference of 1975 and those people who believed in the survival of Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the other hand, President Tudjman stated that Bosnia and Herzegovina was a colonial creation. Bosnia is an old state with a thousand-year history, and Croats from Bosnia did not come from Croatia but are an indigenous group which arrived there in the 7th century from the Carpathian, just like all the other Slavs. Finally, Bosnia and Herzegovina is a rather rare case in Europe because it has the most stable borders within the last 400 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The positions taken by the other faction, the faction other than yours, did those positions fit with the original HDZ BH platform and the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina or not, or don't you have a view?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No. The group that I led, and these were mostly people holding high-ranking government positions and many of the local leaders from Central and Northern Bosnia, fully supported the idea of a sovereign and independent Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the other faction, what I want to know is did the other faction's position fit with or did it violate the HDZ BH platform and all the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: In that period, no one was against the laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but evidently the faction led by Boban and some other people from Herzegovina, which was later joined by many others, was against what we adopted at the party convention in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Boban acting -- and his group acting independently of Zagreb, or not? Or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No. I know very well that they were not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, could you ask the witness -- in his answer, he says that it was fine that Boban did not act independently of Zagreb. Could you tell us, how does he know that, and on which information is this very clear-cut negative answer based?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: First of all, because the policy advocated by Boban was in opposition to the platform adopted at the convention. On the other hand, what Boban was saying was what many people in Zagreb wanted to hear. And finally, when we parted after this meeting, I, together with the officials I had brought with me, and you have to know that we couldn't travel by car because there was a state of war in Croatia, I arrived in Gratz, in Austria, in the government aeroplane of Bosnia and Herzegovina and went to Zagreb from there. So those two groups went their own ways after the meeting. We fled from Zagreb the following morning, in the direction of Austria, and they went out together with the officials from Zagreb that evening. Of course, not with President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I get you to deal with one last extract on the papers? It's a reflection of the other side's point of view. 20/3/JG, please -- sorry, my mistake, 20/4/JG. This is from, as we can see from the previous page, Juric, middle paragraph, beginning "Mislim?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: The first, or the second?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first one.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: [Translation of Serbo-Croatian document as read] "I think that we can truly do everything for a plan, a plan of integration, starting from good preparations for defence to the linking of institutions, the linking in the best sense of that word. At the diplomatic level, our political people in Sarajevo can go on swearing that they are in favour of a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina, as we have said up to now."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next paragraph?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: [Translation of Serbo-Croatian document as read] "I think that this sovereignty will not succeed. No one is supporting it any more. I think that Croatian policy has now at least reached the point where it has to start taking care of its own interests."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were explaining how you fled that meeting, and did you have any feelings as to how things were going to develop with the different factions that now existed?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: In the last two paragraphs, it is evident that they wanted to perform a trick, and that they wanted to go on formally advocating a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina, but they were acting differently, and they did not in fact want it. Unlike them, I truly believed in the future of my homeland, and both as a human being and as a communist dissident, I always openly stated what I was fighting for. I, and most of the people from my faction, did not agree to saying publicly that they were in favour of Bosnia and Herzegovina and secretly working against it. On the other hand, many participants in this meeting left the political scene because the retrograde ideas being advocated there were denied by the events which followed, and that is the Washington Agreement, and the peace between the Croats and the Muslims, and the Dayton Accord, according to which Bosnia and Herzegovina remained a sovereign country with its borders unchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you left that meeting, did you have any concerns for yourself, either your political career or your personal security?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, I was a dissident during communist times, and I never intended to build a political career. But when I was given the honour of leading the Croatian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina, with the help of my associates, I created the best possible political platform. I was concerned, because I knew many people, and besides this, I was the leader of a delegation which brought seven high-ranking officials from Bosnia and Herzegovina there, and it was my responsibility to take them back to Sarajevo. And I was successful in this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 16th of January -- paragraph 21 of the summary -- 16th of January, 1992, did you chair a meeting of the HDZ BH presidency, and at that meeting --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: It's possible, because on the 15th of January, 1992, Croatia gained its independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit Z38, please. I think it's in the pile.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: And we celebrated this event in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see Z38, decisions of the presidency, in English, French, and B/C/S. Number 2 of the decisions --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Please, a Croatian copy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Coming your way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right at the end, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then Item Number 2, we have an English translation which reads to this effect -- perhaps you could follow it in the original. "The HDZ of BH has asked the BH government to include immediately the Croatian dinar into the financial transactions in Bosnia and Herzegovina. If the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina does not act in this manner, the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina will undertake other political measures to protect the Croatian population in Bosnia-Herzegovina from further inflation." Can you make any comment about that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. When we saw what was happening in the former Yugoslavia, when Slovenia and Croatia were intensively preparing for independence, we in Bosnia and Herzegovina tried to protect ourselves from the Yugoslav dinar, which was arriving from Belgrade in vast quantities, with teams of smugglers who bought foreign currency from citizens and took them to Belgrade. The government of Bosnia and Herzegovina printed banknotes, or rather designed banknotes, and had them printed in London, so that we, too, could have our own currency, especially as on the 31st of December, 1991, Croatia abolished the use of the Yugoslav dinar. Unfortunately, the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina was not successful in getting these banknotes printed fast, and when the printing was completed in London, the war broke out, and these banknotes never actually reached Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nothing else on that. I think the next document in the pile is Z2748. I include it simply because you have produced it. I have no comments on it. Please confirm that this is a letter from the head of HDZ BH in Mostar's municipal committee concerning an election of the supreme court -- of a supreme court justice, I think. If I've got it wrong, or if there's a material comment, please make it.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. No, no, no, please, it was our obligation to staff a large number of institutions, including the judicial system. After receiving some recommendations from Mostar, we elected Mr. Ljubomir Zovko as a justice of the constitutional court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we believed this to be a good solution. However, the struggle between the different factions in the Mostar HDZ was very fierce, and I received a letter from the president of the Mostar HDZ in which he objected to this appointment. However, I have to tell the Trial Chamber that this gentleman was later very well received by the same people who objected to his being appointed, and throughout the war, he held a high position in the judiciary of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 22 of the summary: Was there a meeting on the 2nd of February, called by Drago Krpina, in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the purpose of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: As you can see from these documents, the polarisation of the two fractions was growing, and it could no longer be concealed from the public. I was handicapped because I had to deal with affairs of state, I had to attend meetings of the presidency, of the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, inter-party discussions with the SDA and the SDS, talks with the international mediators. And while I was busy doing all this, and so were my associates, they took the opportunity to organise themselves on the ground. The fact that this meeting was held in Siroki Brijeg on the 2nd of February, 1992, and that it was organised from Zagreb, was a blow to the legal leadership and to me personally. I had two plans. One was not to go, and to wait and see what they would decide. And because of the overall situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I would probably have been disciplined by my party. The second plan was to go there and to fight for my political views. I chose the second path. In the meantime, I received information that in Siroki Brijeg, they wanted to challenge the referendum issue, and that they were asking for it to be altered. You should know that at that time the international community, and primarily the European union, required us to apply for the recognition of the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, of which I was a member, sent this application to the European union, and five out of seven members voted in favour of doing so. Only the two Serbian representatives did not support this application. Since there was no inter-ethnic consensus, the European Community insisted that a referendum should be held in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The question was, "Are you in favour of an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina of equal citizens and peoples?" At the meeting in Siroki Brijeg, a high-ranking delegation of Zagreb was present, consisting of Stipe Mesic, Perica Juric, and Vice Vukojevic, and I chaired the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the objective of the Zagreb delegation, so far as your position was concerned?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: The delegation which attended the meeting in Siroki Brijeg did not say what their aim was. On the contrary, we greeted each other warmly, as if this were some kind of routine meeting, but a few years later, Stipe Mesic told me that the task he had been given was to get me dismissed at the meeting in Siroki Brijeg. However, when he saw the support I had in the hall, he did not try to carry out this task.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the event, how did the meeting end? I'm sorry, by whom had Stipe Mesic been given that particular task? I should have asked you that.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I don't know. We can only suppose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you by whom he was given the task?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: He said that the leadership in Zagreb had asked him to do this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The meeting ended with what, so far as your position was concerned?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: The meeting was interrupted. Because out of the 41 members who took the floor, 39 were from Herceg-Bosna, and some of these accused me openly as a traitor of Croatian interests, as a person who, cooperating with the Muslim party, had brought the Croats into an inferior position. One of them, Jozo Maric, stood up and said that the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina refused to be ruled by the Turks for another 500 years. In the meantime, many representatives from Bosnia who lived a long way off left the meeting, saying to me, "Mr. President, we support you, but it's late, we have to get home." You should know that at that time, there were many Serbian checkpoints in Bosnia, and that the roads were unsafe. So I prepared for this meeting especially, and I decided not to eat anything at the meeting. However, later, I felt ill, and I can tell you later on what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you were in hospital for some -- 20 days?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: You see, when I saw that they wanted to outvote me and that they wanted to challenge the referendum as the most important document for the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina and for the Croatian people in this country, because if the referendum was not successful, Bosnia and Herzegovina would remain in Milosevic's Yugoslavia, I interrupted the meeting and told them, "Gentlemen, you can go your way, and I'll go mine." I left, although they all tried to keep me there. Mesic, too, of course. However, I am not a person who makes decisions easily, and I knew that on the basis of the statute of the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I had paralysed the further work of the gathering. I said that I would resign, and the statute of the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina states that, should the president say that he is going to resign, he still remains the resigning president, and for his resignation to be either accepted or rejected, a convention has to be called. It was quite clear to me that they wanted to sabotage the referendum, and Milosevic probably was interested in Western Herzegovina and the Cazim region -- he would have given those areas to someone else because they were not territories which could be governed easily. It later became evident that this was their intention, when they meet in Livno a week later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's pause there a moment. I'm going to come back to the constitution and the document that evidences it right at the end, for completeness, but can you look now, please, at -- Livno was -- Livno, tell us about the date of that meeting, and what happened there?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: On the 9th of February, 1992, those same people met in Livno and ordered a new referendum question. Generally speaking, the idea was that Bosnia should be a tripartite community, and this was requested and submitted to the election commission, or rather referendum commission, which refused it on formal grounds as this request had arrived too late, and its authors did not meet the conditions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you look, please, then, at Document 2749, which I hope is in the Court's pile. The third sheet shows that this is dated the 12th of February. Can you tell us what this document is, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: At the time, Lord Carrington was conducting very intensive talks, and he was to be joined by Mr. Cyrus Vance, with all the leaders of ethnic parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the end, when they were not satisfied, when they were not happy with the outcome of those meetings, they asked for each of the ethnic parties to draw up a text as a summary of their idea of the future independent state. More specifically, this text is the SDA proposal. It is of great consequence, because it takes note of the request of the Croats to have a chamber of peoples in the parliament in which representatives of individual ethnic communities would have the right of veto in cases of a major national interest, rather ethnic interest. We did not have it in communism, but that was part of our programme, and I can tell you that today in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that in the Federation and in Bosnia-Herzegovina there is a chamber of peoples. So we and the SDS submitted similar documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that reflects what was going on on the 12th of February. You, I think, were still in hospital. Did you write to President Tudjman on the 14th of February?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does a copy of that letter exist, or to tell us about it, are you dependent on memory?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I believe there is a copy of that letter which I gave. The letter is original, and it is very important, because the eve before that I went through a crisis; that is, after 11 days of fighting for my life, I did remain alive. And as soon as I could summon enough strength to sit at a table, I did sit so and wrote a letter to Mr. Tudjman, a letter in which I warned him that he had to bring pressure to bear on those -- when I say "those," then I mean those who did not abide by the political platform of the Bosnia and Herzegovina and HDZ -- and in which I also indicated that if the referendum failed, that Bosnia and Herzegovina would then remain in rump Yugoslavia, and that that would be the greatest of the disasters for the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I also wrote that he should recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he subsequently heeded to my advice, because in this manner he would at long last show that he was not the one to partition Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you wrote to him, did you get any acknowledgement from him, or any reply, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No. Quite the contrary. Nobody called from Zagreb while I was in the hospital. I asked [indiscernible] that [indiscernible] call me, offering me treatment in Vienna, and nobody dialled my number from Croatia. I received very many telegrams from citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina of all ethnic origins, in which they wished me to get well soon, and then a day after I sent this letter, little Perica Juric called me from Zagreb, asking me to call him. I think it was cynical on his part, but I clearly don't want to talk about my personal problems here. It was really beyond belief that the whole European press wrote that I had been poisoned, and yet from Zagreb, from my own party, from my own political partners, nobody bothered about me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I just backtrack a little? There is a document in the pile dealing with the meeting at Livno. It's Z45. Can the witness just see it? Although he wasn't present at the meeting, he may have seen the document and be able to confirm it.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I cannot authenticate this document, but all I can say is that here is a standard HDZ form. And I can confirm the question from Livno, which was carried by all the newspapers and all the other media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at the other document, there are a couple of signatures, not terribly clear. Do you recognise them?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I see. Secretary and initiative clerk; Boban, vice-president of the HDZ; Santic, another vice-president; Ivan Markesic, general secretary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise either of those signatures?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I have only two, Andzelka Stojic and Ivan Markesic's. I couldn't really claim that these are their signatures. You would have to ask them. I don't think there is any secret in this. The most important thing is the question was publicised and publicly printed, so that there was nothing secret about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You left hospital, and you told us about one letter you received. Did you receive a letter from Markesic on the 19th of February? I'm sorry, I --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: What is the letter about? Markesic was in Sarajevo with me, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll just show you the letter.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. At a session in Lisbon, I was being prepared, and with the ecoutier, who was the mediator, the negotiators of the HDZ, the SDA, and the SDS were to attend that meeting. The secretary general, Ivan Markesic, after I summoned enough strength to go back to work, sent a proposal to Zagreb that I should head the delegation of Bosnia-Herzegovinian HDZ. The next day, Stipe Mesic replied that allegedly I wasn't feeling all too well and the delegation should comprise Boban, Miro Lasic, Stanic, and that was the delegation that went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at Z2754, is that the letter from Mesic that you just spoke of?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a meeting on the 15th of March called by Krpina in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, but there is a vacuum here, we've got a void here. May I explain something?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Because it is very important, you know. After I left the hospital and generally up until I left Siroki Brijeg, I had a very clear political direction, as the statute was on my side and they could not dismiss me without holding a convention. Then I went around and started promoting the referendum, and I believe that was a historic moment in Bosnia because I enjoyed absolute support of the Catholic Church, and we, the Croats, contributed to the referendum held on the 29th of February or 1st of March succeeding. I must say that the largest percentage of Croats voted for the referendum. In terms of structure, Croats had 17,3 per cent share of the population, but because the population was -- they were of older generations, so their share in the electorate was larger. On the other hand, the Muslims accounted for a very large share of the population, but the population is younger, so that they were represented on the electorate with a smaller number of people. In contrast, a considerable number of Serbs also voted for an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina. Sixty-six per cent who voted for an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina was seen by Jacques Santer as an excellent result, and he personally told me at a luncheon that in the western countries, less people than that turn out to vote. Even though I was very happy that we had won our independence, I yet knew that not all was formally over with the HDZ. Why is that? As the president, I believed, when I began to promote the referendum, that if I won in the referendum, then I would hold a convention of the party and remove the entire referendum stream, and if I lose in the referendum, I intended to withdraw. However, I won the referendum. The Croat people offered their whole-hearted vote for an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina, but Zagreb never permitted to hold the convention. That is why the meeting in Bugojno was organised on the 15th of March, and I was not even invited to it, to be quite honest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that meeting --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that meeting, who was elected acting president?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milenko Berkic was elected. Otherwise, he was a member of the last Communist government. However, it was a bypass of sorts, because he was to be dismissed and replaced by Boban. You probably want to know why couldn't they immediately bring Boban after me. Well, quite simply because I enjoyed the great trust of all citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and representatives of the International Community, notably ambassadors of major states to Yugoslavia, at that time already saw that that separatist line was not good either for the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina or for the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, in the course of the war which commenced in early April '92 in Bosnia-Herzegovina, things radically changed, and sometime at some meeting in Posusje or wherever, Boban, at long last, became the wartime president of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just conclude with the appointment of Boban. That happened on the 24th of October, did it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you invited to be at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No. Had they invited me, I would have gone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if anything, happened to you or what, if anything, was done of a formal nature about your position on that meeting or at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes, they then decided to dismiss me from the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That decision was unlawful because I was elected ad persona, I mean, to the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is. Of all the 42 candidates for the presidency, I won the relative majority of all votes, which means that representatives of other ethnic communities had also voted for me. However, their request would have been immaterial, would have been irrelevant, had not the president of the presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, not concluded a separate contract with President Tudjman and Mate Boban. If you care to, I can briefly recount it to you, because that was an event which produced a tremendous effect on the future fate of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, perhaps we could hear something about that agreement.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. On the 19th of December, '92, according to the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I was to become its president. Namely, pursuant to our constitution, a man could not hold the office of the president for more than two years. Izetbegovic's term was expiring on the 19th of December, '92. Tudjman, Zagreb, and Herceg-Bosna could not accept -- could not agree that I become the president of that state because they knew that I would very consistently pursue the policy which I had advocated from the outset. Because of that, there was a meeting in Zagreb between Tudjman and Izetbegovic in which he said that Izetbegovic should remove Kljuic and that Izetbegovic would then continue as the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Needless to say, Izetbegovic wanted that, but Tudjman told him, "But you've agreed with me, but your real partner, your true counterpart, is Mate Boban." So Izetbegovic goes to Grude, and that was truly a sensation, because until that time Izetbegovic used always to censor or to condemn Boban's policy. I did not know about the substance of the Grude meeting, and I was to learn it only a few years later. But when Izetbegovic returned to the presidency, we met, and I laughed, "Who are you, the president of this state, going to the smallest municipality to conduct negotiations," because Grude was absolutely the smallest municipality in the state. And Izetbegovic, you know, slyly said, "Well, you have to talk with everyone." But what happened? I really did not feel up to dealing politically with such a man. I mean there was HDZ and Boban, but I did not want to leave the presidency because I had fought for it personally in the elections. However, this was a procedure in which they were not requesting only my resignation, my dismissal, but also the dismissal of the prime minister, Jure Pelivan, and explicitly asking that Miro Lasic substitute for me. He had never been on the electoral list and, therefore, pursuant to our constitution, could not become the president. However, to put Izetbegovic in a situation to publicly violate the constitution or support me, I wrote a letter to the presidency and acceding my place in the presidency to Miro Lasic. At the same time, Mila Ekmescic replaced Jure Pelivan, and then when Izetbegovic accepted -- admitted Miro Lasic in the presidency, they overthrew the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because pursuant to the constitution, if I had properly resigned, then a person figuring the third on the electoral list would have taken my place, and that was Ivo Komisic. But when he violated the constitution, succumbed to Tudjman's pressure, then Tudjman ordered all high officials of the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina to leave their offices and move either to Herceg-Bosna or to Zagreb. Thus, in the history of Bosnia, there is a disgrace that the prime minister left without saying goodbye, he did not resign, he fled from the country, and that Miro Lasic went as a member of the presidency and with him another member, Boras, and all this was done so as to represent the lawful presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina as Muslim. Then when Tudjman and Izetbegovic met in Zagreb the next time, and this is what Izetbegovic told me, then Tudjman said, "Well, don't you know, Mr. Izetbegovic, that you're not the president of the state? Don't you know your own constitution? You are the president of the Muslims," that kind of policy whereby Bosnia-Herzegovina was to be torn apart, and Izetbegovic, brought to negotiate as representatives of the Muslims only, was the most dangerous of all. Ten months later, under the pressure of the international public and the big powers, a lawful presidency was reinstated in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I was also on it, and it remained in power until the end of 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The appointment of Boban, in your judgement, organised by whom?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, he couldn't become the president. Well, presumably he must have had a number of people who were supporting him, but he wouldn't have been able to become the president without the support of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A few documents that I've overlooked, I think, are probably in the Court's bundle which I ought to just tidy up. If the Court has 2750 and 2751, can we just look at those, please, just for completeness. It's my oversight not to have put these in the right sequence. Also 2752, if you've got it. 2750, what's that, please? It's dated the 12th of February.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: This is a mix-up, a confusion which set in after the Livno issue, because people around were asking for an explanation and seeking that explanation from the general secretary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 2751, another letter from the Opstina --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Well, I think this is a humane -- a very warmly-written letter which shows that my poisoning at Siroki Brijeg was not accidental. The president of the municipal government simply sends me a letter and wishes me to get well quickly and tells me not really to think too much of the events of Siroki Brijeg. He says, "Please realise that the toll passes but people stay."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 2752, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: This is my letter to President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the hospital?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've given us a summary of it already. Without reading passages out loud, just check if there are no other parts of it that you want to refer to, turning the pages if you need to.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No, I already said what was most important in the referendum, independence of Bosnia, the pressure brought on those who were supporting the referendum. I also indicated what would be the future of Bosnia if we avoided the referendum, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two other documents that have yet to be distributed, I think, 2759 and 2760. I don't think they are in the pile. Copies are coming, in enough numbers for the Court, the Defence, and the witness. 2759, please. Tell us, please, what 2759 is. You can see it's dated Zagreb, 1990.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, yes. This is from the first general Congress of the HDZ held in Zagreb in early 1990 where the leadership of the Croatian HDZ was elected and later on this will lead to their election victory in the spring of the same year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you, I think, go to page -- on page 22 of this document, what is there?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: This is the general statute of the HDZ, statute of the Croatian Democratic Community in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you now take Document 2760. What publication is this?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: The publication is called "Bosna and Herzegovina" -- I cannot see from which paper because a number of newspapers had this type of size. It could be Zagreb, it could be --
