utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the bottom of the page, which isn't on the ELMO at the moment --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the party paper of the Zagreb HDZ. The Croatian Democratic Community, as a party, issued its own paper, and this is an excerpt from that paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if you turn to the second sheet, please, the right-hand column, the second fresh paragraph, beginning "u sedmoj", a bit higher up, please. Yes, that's the one there, in the middle of the page now. Thank you very much. Can you just read out that paragraph for us, please?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: "The Congress was then addressed by Neven Jurica, Muhamed Zulic and Dalibor Brozovic. Their speeches reflected the idea that Bosnia-Hercegovina had to go to Europe, and the quickest and best way was through Croatia."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next paragraph?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: In the seventh point of the agenda, the BH HDZ Statute was adopted. It was presented by Miljenko Zagar. He said that the statute was the same with the HDZ statute of the Republic of Croatia, because all of the HDZ were one single movement. In the BiH HDZ statute, the changes in article 4, 8, 43, and 72, were proposed in order to adapt to the political terminology in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the statute and the changes were adopted by acclamation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that apart from those clauses, the statute that we've produced as Exhibit 2759 should apply for the Bosnia-Herzegovina party as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No. After I was elected president, I had to reregister the party at a superior court in Sarajevo, and among others, I changed what was there before; that is, the HDZ for Bosnia and Herzegovina and I substituted "by HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina." So that we were registered as an independent political party. And of course we continued to maintain very close relations with the HDZ in Zagreb, and I have to say that they have helped the HDZ in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But apart from that important change in title, the clause is subject to what is said in the official newspaper, the clauses remain the same for both Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: The concept of the party was the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a small matter of detail, at some stage, did President Tudjman offer you a post overseas?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that President Tudjman realised that he could not manipulate me politically, that I could not change my political views, given that I had been a dissident for so many years, that I had very clear views, and then he behaved in a gentlemanly manner, and he invited me to either come and work with him in Zagreb, or he also offered me an ambassadorship in Argentina. And the same thing happened in Bosnia. I said, "Perhaps I look like an ambassador, but I don't think that you can really get rid of me that way."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To be ambassador in South America, this was for which country? Ambassador for?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: Yes, to be the ambassador of the Republic of Croatia. And I said, "Mr. Tudjman, I cannot be your ambassador, because I am going to be placing our own ambassadors of my own country to those countries."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, finally, paragraph 30 of the summary, I think you have a Bosnia-Herzegovinian passport, don't you? Do you have a Croatian passport?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No, unfortunately. And today, it's a handicap. But both myself and my family have passports of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because as a politician, as a person who is fighting for the equality of Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, cannot hold other passports. And privately, perhaps, it would have been -- it would be much more pleasant for me to have spent the wartime as an ambassador abroad than spending it at home through the war, and -- you know, to have to sustain all the consequences of the war. But those people who were against me, especially those who harmed me so much, I harbour no ill feelings towards such people to date. Many of these people should be understood in a particular way, because in such a crucial historical moment, they were unable to reach the right decisions, and especially those younger ones became victims of a policy which was conducted from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One matter of detail I haven't dealt with is paragraph 30 of the summary, but you can deal with this quite shortly. In the conflict, were there leadership meetings, including one at Graz on the 7th of February, 1992?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: There were several meetings in Graz. Manolic, Karadzic, and then Boban and Karadzic, and once even Borac was there. These were all attempts to contact the Serbian side and reach an agreement with them. And I have to say that people who led Herceg-Bosna at the time, the top people, I have to say, had continuous contacts with Karadzic's people throughout the war. We watched on Serbian television when the government of Herceg-Bosna, in the middle of the war, twice officially visited, once Banja Luka and another time Herceg Novi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dario Kordic, you've spoken about the meeting which you attended and of which the minutes are available. Did you meet him personally other than at that sort of meeting?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: No, we never saw each other after 27 December -- that is, after the 2nd of February, in Mostar. I was not in Bugojno. The war had started. I lived in Sarajevo. And I would just like to add that he was not part of those delegations which went to Herceg Novi and Banja Luka. If that is of any interest to you, he was not a member of those delegations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, just back on those meetings: At the time that those meetings were going on, they were, of course, at war one with another; is that right? Meetings in Graz and so on?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC
utterances.text: I don't know about those things, apart from the reports in the media and what Mesic told me. But the international news organisations reported when Manolic first met, and he confirmed it, too, for me. And there was a Boban/Karadzic meeting in Graz, and it was then represented as if an agreement was reached where they agreed that if there were any Croats left in Sarajevo, that Karadzic would take care of them, and if there were any Serbs in Mostar, it was Boban who was going to take care of them. But I'm talking about a development of the situation which led to three catastrophic errors regarding the Croatian population. One is against the population itself, one against Bosnia and Herzegovina, and thirdly against the Republic of Croatia, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Court said that 4.15 was its time for ending today, and I think that is the last question I have to ask. If we are going over to tomorrow morning, if I could just technically keep examination-in-chief open in case there's something I've omitted, I'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the position about cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's been no agreement. I've made the point to my learned friends opposite that this is no doubt a witness in relation to whom their case will have been clear for a long time. He is a central figure in the history, and the documents that have been produced -- many of them simply for completeness and because they've been brought, provided ahead of the time that they would normally get them -- may not themselves generate any specific cross-examination. But we would ask that the case continues in the normal way. This witness can be here tomorrow. As to any other days, I'm not so sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you made any inquiries?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, we have, yes. Can we possibly conveniently just go into private session, rather than full closed session? As we are discussing timetable matters, it would be safer, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. But before we do, there are some documents which were handed up which haven't been referred to. There's one, 1437, which is a newspaper report which has been translated into English. I don't know if you want to rely on that at all or whether we can hand it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we defer all that until tomorrow morning? I'll make a final decision overnight. I've been attempting to prune documents to some extent, but nevertheless, if they're official documents, I think they're better produced by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the witness will be required, in any event, will he, tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, certainly, if -- I think he will be required. I don't know what the Defence position is, but it may be preferable if we just deal with that in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go into private session. (Trial Chamber confers) (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
